intro: How Class 4 National Insurance applies to self-employed profits, when Class 2 is treated as paid, and who can pay voluntary Class 2 or Class 3 contributions.
explanation:
## Class 4 is charged on profits, not on turnover, and only above a lower limit

Profits are your self-employed income after deducting your expenses. No Class 4 National Insurance is due up to {fact:ni_lower_profits_limit}. Above that, {fact:ni_class4_main_rate} is charged on profits up to {fact:ni_upper_profits_limit}, and {fact:ni_class4_upper_rate} on anything higher. Most people pay it through Self Assessment, alongside Class 2.

A few groups follow different rules. People who examine, moderate, invigilate or write exam questions are handled differently: their Special Class 4 is arranged with the National Insurance office rather than through a Self Assessment return. Landlords need to check whether National Insurance applies to their rental income at all. Ministers of religion with no salary or stipend, and people who invest for themselves or others without making it a business and without a fee or commission, do not have to pay, though they can choose to make voluntary contributions.

## A year can count towards the State Pension even when no Class 2 is paid

When profits reach {fact:ni_small_profits_threshold}, Class 2 is treated as having been paid, so nothing is owed and the National Insurance record is still protected. This matters because the Class 4 limit is higher: profits between the two figures owe no Class 4 and still earn a qualifying year.

Below {fact:ni_small_profits_threshold}, nothing has to be paid, but the year may leave a gap in the record. Paying voluntary Class 2 at {fact:ni_class2_voluntary_rate} a week closes it.

## Voluntary contributions fill gaps, but not everyone gains from them

Where self-employed profits fall short of {fact:ni_small_profits_threshold}, either Class 2 or Class 3 can be paid. Class 3 costs {fact:ni_class3_voluntary_rate} a week. Some self-employed people in particular jobs, including examiners and landlords who are eligible to pay Class 2, can also pay voluntarily even though their Class 2 is not treated as paid.

Gaps matter because a State Pension usually needs at least 10 qualifying years. Voluntary payments do not always raise a pension, for example where someone was contracted out, and they cannot be paid where the record has no gap. The State Pension forecast shows whether a payment would help.

The rate for a voluntary payment is normally the current one. Class 2 for the previous tax year and Class 3 for the previous two tax years are charged at those years' original rates, while older years cost the current rate. A gap can be filled only for the last 6 tax years, and the cut-off date is 5 April.
meta_description: Class 4 National Insurance on self-employed profits is {fact:ni_class4_main_rate} above {fact:ni_lower_profits_limit} a year. How Class 2, voluntary Class 2 and Class 3 contributions work.
